title: Leads still being pursued in [unclear] murder
author: Beth L. Chester
text:
Is there a random killer on the loose — one who kills for no reason? Early in the investigation into Levi Frady’s murder, officials tried to ease parents’ fears that someone might be stalking Forsyth County children.

Just days after the 11-year-old’s body was found, Dawson County Sheriff Billy Carlisle told worried parents that statistics in child homicide cases indicate that young victims usually die at the hands of someone they know.

But with time passing without an arrest in the murder, Levi’s maternal grandmother questions whether other children in Forsyth are safe from Levi’s assailant.

In a written statement, Janice Hamby poses the question: “Are your children safe at the bus stop? There’s a killer out there somewhere,” she writes. “They have killed once, and it will be easier the next time.”

Even when Carlisle generalized about child murders, he was quick to add that no judgment was being made about Levi’s murder specifically, saying he did not know for certain whether Levi had known his killer.

The grandmother wonders whether parents shouldn’t be taking extra precautions until the murderer is found, saying she thinks it’s possible Levi did not know his killer. “We just don’t know right now. It could have happened either way,” she said.

Because of the uncertainty, she doesn’t want parents to have a false sense of security. “I don’t want to scare anyone. I just want them to be cautious until the murderer is found. If one child can be killed, another child could be killed.

“A child should be allowed to play,” she writes, but points out that parents should not assume the person living next door or down the street is safe. “Do you (really) know your neighbor?”

[Continues under MURDER on page 2A, not supplied.]

title: Timeline: The Levi Frady Mystery
text:
Oct. 22, 1997

• 3:30 p.m. - 4:12 p.m. Levi Frady, 11, departs from North Forsyth Middle School and arrives at his Burruss Mill Road home after getting off the school bus. Note: Levi’s twin sister Laci remains at school awaiting her mother, Marilyn Parkman, to pick her up at approximately 5:30 p.m.

• 4:12 p.m. Levi calls his mother at her workplace in Alpharetta, and tells her that he is going over to visit a friend on Noah Road and is also going by another friend’s residence. His mother tells Levi to be home by 6:30 p.m.

• 4:12 p.m. - 5 p.m. A couple walking on Little Mill Road sees Levi riding his bicycle past their driveway heading in the direction of another couple’s residence (on Little Mill Road). They observe that Levi has his book bag strapped on his back.

• 4:15 p.m. - 4:30 p.m. Another neighborhood resident sees Levi riding his bicycle traveling down Picklesimer Road.

• 4:30 - 5 p.m. Another neighborhood resident sees Levi riding his bike in the direction of Levi’s friend’s house.

• 4:40 p.m. - 5:45 p.m. Levi and his friend (friend #1) ride their bicycles over to another friend’s (friend #2) residence and play on the trampoline. During the visit, friend #2 invites Levi to go out to eat with his family. Friend #1 does not have the money to go and declines. Levi does have money with him and calls his residence to talk with his mother. She is not at home.

• 4:55 p.m. His mother leaves work en route to school to pick up her daughter.

• 5:30 p.m. - 5:45 p.m. Levi’s mother and sister arrive home bringing carry-out food from a local fast food restaurant.

• 5:45 p.m. - 6 p.m. Friend #2 and his family leave their residence en route to the restaurant to eat. Levi and friend #1 leave the residence at the same time en route back to the residence of friend #1. Note: Levi leaves his book bag on the patio of the residence of friend #2.

• 6:25 p.m. - 6:35 p.m. A witness is traveling down Little Mill Road in his Ford Bronco pulling a trailer. As he is approaching Frog’s Creek, he meets a beige F-150 truck followed by an Oldsmobile or Pontiac station wagon with ladders and a ladder rack. He stops to let the truck and station wagon go by. As he continues traveling, he meets two boys coming down a hill on their bicycles on the right side of the road. He then continues up the hill and sees a man walking down the hill on the left side of the road. The man has been picking up cans. (See composite sketch A)

• 6 p.m. - 6:38 p.m. Levi remains with friend #1, and at 6:38 p.m., they travel over to another residence to use the telephone. Levi’s friend remains outside the residence, and Levi calls home and talks with his sister. Note: Levi’s mother is in the bathtub and tells her daughter to tell Levi to come straight home. Levi says that he does not want to ride his bicycle home because it is getting dark and Levi mentions being afraid of some of the dogs he would encounter on his way home.

• 6:45 p.m. - 6:50 p.m. Levi leaves the residence of friend #1 on his bicycle traveling in the direction of Little Mill Road. Levi travels in this direction to avoid encountering the dogs on the other route, which would have been Picklesimer Road (the direction he initially came when traveling to his friend’s house after 4:12 p.m.)

• 6:50 p.m. A resident sees Levi traveling on his bike down Little Mill Road heading in the direction of the residence of friend #2. Note: the resident observed a small black dog following Levi.

• 6:52 p.m. - 7 p.m. A motorist, a stranger in the community who was lost, drives past a man described as being between 35 and 60 years old, having grayish black or light brown hair (scraggly and unkept). She observes that the man is wearing possibly blue jeans and a white or light colored shirt with the sleeves rolled up. She stops and attempts to ask the man for directions. The man does not respond to her when she says, “Mister.” The man walks off into the woods immediately after she speaks. The location where the man walks off into the woods is located at a resident’s driveway, which is within a few hundred feet of where Levi’s bike was ultimately found. She did not see a bicycle lying on the side of the road in that area during that time.

• 7 p.m. Levi’s mother calls Levi’s friend’s residence looking for her son but gets no answer.

• 7 p.m. - 7:15 p.m. Levi’s mother and sister leave their residence en route to look for Levi. Note: The mother’s boyfriend, Tim Tatum, pulls into the driveway as they are leaving. She tells her boyfriend that she is going to look for Levi because he has not come home yet. During this search, Levi’s sister sees a bike that looks like the one belonging to her brother lying on the side of the road at a driveway on Little Mill Road about a half mile from Levi’s home. She tells her mother, but her mother does not hear her. The mother travels to Levi’s friend’s house and after checking there, returns home. Levi’s sister does not mention seeing the bike again.

• 7:34 p.m. Levi’s mother and sister are back at their residence, and Levi’s sister calls her friend and tells her that Levi has not come home.

8:01 p.m. The family of Levi’s friend #2 purchases items at the Kmart in Cumming after the family went out to eat and writes a check.

Oct. 23, 1997

• 2 a.m. Levi’s mother wakes up to check on Levi. Levi is not home and she again leaves her residence in her vehicle and drives around on the road looking for Levi. She does not see the bicycle at a resident’s driveway.

• 5:15 a.m. A resident leaves for work and sees Levi’s bicycle at the end of his driveway on the edge adjacent to Little Mill Road.

• 6 a.m. A resident leaves for work and sees Levi’s bicycle in the same location as her husband did. Note: Neither of the residents moved the bicycle.

• 6:45 a.m. The residents’ children leave their residence and walk down to the end of the driveway to wait for the school bus. They see the bicycle at the end of the driveway adjacent to Little Mill Road and place it in the ditch alongside the driveway (where it is ultimately found).

• 7:02 a.m. Levi’s sister talks to her father by phone but does not tell him that Levi is missing.

• 7:30 a.m. Levi’s mother telephones the parents of Levi’s friend and tells them she is looking for Levi.

• 7:50 a.m. Levi’s mother returns to Levi’s friend’s residence and again looks for Levi. Note: During this time, Levi’s grandfather and other relatives are out looking for Levi. They find the bicycle in the ditch located adjacent to a driveway and pick the bike up and take it over to Levi’s mother’s house. The family discusses the matter and decides to take the bicycle back to its location before law enforcement arrives.

• 8 a.m. Levi’s mother files a missing person report with the Forsyth County Sheriff’s Office on her son Levi.

• 9:30 a.m. Levi’s mother calls her boyfriend at his place of employment and tells him that Levi is missing. He leaves work and comes to the search area.

• 10:15 a.m. Levi’s mother contacts Levi’s father, Milton Frady, and apprises him of the situation.

• 10:30 a.m. Ground search in the Little Mill area begins.

• 2 p.m. The body of Levi Frady is found in Dawson Forest Game Management Area by hunters. The area is near an abandoned Lockheed plant. Levi had been shot three times.

• 10:48 p.m. A hunter from Dawson Forest is interviewed, and he gives a description of a small blue truck with a white camper being seen in an area close to the crime scene at approximately 10 a.m. this same date. He also gives a description of a man dressed in a dress shirt and attire, which seemed out of place in Dawson Forest. (See composite sketch B)
notes: No byline or underlying timeline-source credit visible on supplied page. This is a newspaper timeline, not an authenticated GBI record. Neighboring LEVI article continues from 1A, absent. Sketch A shows two views of a man, Sketch B another man; no suspect identity inferred. Reading order reconstructed across six columns. All witness roles unnamed except named family. Date headings/clock readings retained without inventing timezone. Spelling “unkept” preserved.

title: LEVI — continuation from 1A (opening headline unavailable)
text:
[Continued from page 1A; supplied text begins mid-sentence.]

a personality profile early on of the type of person who may have committed the murder, but he won’t disclose any details.

He also wouldn’t say whether any DNA evidence was recovered from the scene that could link the crime to an individual. In recent years, several unsolved crimes have been cracked thanks to new DNA databases containing the genetic data of felony offenders.

Cagle will say that investigators are carefully re-examining the physical evidence, which he says has been painstakingly preserved.

“Forensic capabilities have changed, so we’re reviewing the evidence to see if we need to resubmit it,” Cagle said.

The entire Frady file — all 66 volumes — has been getting a new look in recent months, part of a routine review done in all unsolved murders, Cagle said.

“Although it’s what I would call a cold case, it’s still an active case,” he said. “It’s not a closed matter. We’re still working on it.”

Carlisle, who was sheriff at the time, said the case is “very frustrating. It’s the only unsolved homicide in the county.”

“I think about it all the time, especially this time of year,” Carlisle said. “If we could solve it, it would be a tremendous relief for me.”

Anyone with any information about the abduction and murder of Levi Frady is asked to call the Georgia Bureau of Investigation at (888) 233-5680.

title: Sheriff Hendrix replies to resident’s concerns
author: Denny Hendrix
text:
DEAR EDITOR:

A letter appeared in your Sunday, April 26 issue written by the aunt of Levi Frady, the 11 year-old Forsyth County boy whose body was found in Dawson Forest in October. I wanted to address some concerns she raised in this letter.

First of all, I want to assure Ms. Patrick and all of the relatives and friends of this child that the Sheriff’s Office is doing everything humanly possible to apprehend the person or persons responsible for his murder. Although Levi Frady did live in Forsyth County, the crime of murder did occur in Dawson County. Under the law, a crime must be investigated by the county authorities in the county where it occurred. When more than one county is involved in a crime, a common practice in law enforcement is to ask for assistance from a larger agency. That agency in this case is the Georgia Bureau of Investigation (G.B.I.

The G.B.I. is now the lead investigating agency, with Dawson County assisting. The Forsyth County Sheriff’s Office is only a support agency in this investigation, unlike the investigation of the decapitated man. In that case, we were the lead investigating agency. At the beginning of the investigation, all of the evidence was located in Forsyth County.

We now have an investigator who is working with the G.B.I. on a full-time basis, following up on leads given to him. The G.B.I. and Dawson County authorities are also very concerned about the murder of this child and have done a professional job with the investigation.

Also in this letter, mention was made of the disagreements between the County Commission and the Sheriff taking time away from this investigation. The Commissioners have been nothing but supportive throughout the investigation. They contributed money towards a reward fund and Chairman Bill Jenkins has also verbally given me permission to use whatever overtime hours we may need to solve this horrible crime. In no way has any disagreement between the Commissioners and the Sheriff hampered the investigation of the murder of Levi Frady.

The death of Levi Frady never leaves my mind. Unfortunately, there are no deadlines on investigations. Many times crimes are solved only when the perpetrator’s conscious begins to wear down and he or she must tell someone to alleviate themselves of the heavy burden of guilt.

I promise we will continue to work diligently to solve this murder. One day someone will be brought to justice and pay for the crime that has been committed against one of God’s children.

Denny Hendrix
Sheriff, Forsyth County
notes: Signed public letter: class B for author’s stated role/position, not class A investigative proof and not independent legal guidance. Column order crosses bottom-left columns to top of fourth letter column. Adjacent letter policy and unrelated letters excluded. The “all evidence ... Forsyth” sentence occurs while comparing the decapitated-man investigation; it is not silently attributed to Levi’s case. Missing closing parenthesis after G.B.I. and printed “conscious” retained. LETTERS p.15A refers to neighboring material; Hendrix signature appears here.

title: FRIENDS — continuation from 1A (opening headline unavailable)
text:
[Continued from page 1A; supplied text begins mid-word/sentence.]

est and best friends, and Watters says Levi was just a normal 11-year-old boy with best friends of his own.

Sometimes meeting in groups — sometimes talking one-on-one, Watters says the most important thing is for she and other counselors to let the children share their feelings.

“We do more listening than talking, and the children talk about how they feel and share memories about Levi. We want to know what life is like for them now.”

Watters says “children go through the grieving process differently than do adults:” Because Levi’s friends are so young, she says “this may be the first personal loss — where they truly miss someone — which many children have ever experienced.”

Initially, the grief is “on the surface” she said, but now it surfaces in “more subtle ways.”

When children lose someone close to them, Watters says it is common for them to channel their sadness in other areas: “They will act out, have less self control or be angrier,” she says, “and they may not even be aware that they are really feeling sad.”

So, parents and teachers can sometimes mistake the change in behavior and not realize “it’s really grief.”

To help, Watters says counselors try to “reassure children that their feelings are natural” and have assigned many of the students peer and adult mentors.

Watters says the mentors undergo thorough background screenings and are available to “spend time with the kids and do special things” to help them cope.

Although she describes the atmosphere as one of “edginess right now,” she doesn’t see the “fear and shock” so apparent in the early aftermath of Levi’s slaying.

“They would like to know what happened — to know why, but mostly they just talk about missing Levi and what he was like.”

Even though Watters says most of the children don’t seem overly fearful, she says many seem “frustrated” that their parents are afraid to let them go outside and play as they did before.

“Their lifestyles have changed,” she said. “Whereas kids used to run loose and do what they wanted, now they can’t play in the woods, and are therefore more restricted.”

Watters says the school has no immediate plans for a memorial service for Levi, although she expects some type of permanent memorial to his life will eventually be designated.

“Right now, we’re trying to get some distance between the children and Levi’s death and let things normalize. To hold a service at this point, she says, would be too upsetting. “Adults can handle that, but children can’t.”
notes: Watters’s first name and article byline absent; identity left source-scoped. Apparent quotation punctuation in last paragraph retained as printed, not repaired. No school memorial assumed completed. Printed page clearly Nov. 28, 1997 despite OCR 1987.

title: PRECINCT — continuation from 1A (opening headline unavailable)
text:
Hendrix said community reaction has been excellent.

The precinct receives dozens of walk-ins each day, and provides citizens with an alternative to going to the jail or having a deputy come to their house, said Hendrix.

During the precinct’s opening ceremony, Hendrix said he would like to have a permanent precinct opened in the north end of the county by the end of 1998.

But he said the Frady murder has increased the need for more law enforcement presence immediately.

The temporary precinct will give law enforcement a place to coordinate their efforts on the murder investigation.

Patrols in the north end have already been increased, said Hendrix. A temporary precinct will enable the extra deputies to save time by not driving to headquarters in Cumming before and after each shift.

Commissioner Andy Anderson was asked to help look for a location, said the sheriff.

During the opening of Precinct 1, Anderson said he fully supported the idea of precincts and would help anyway he could to open a permanent one in the county’s north end.

Hendrix said he still hopes to have another precinct open by the end of next year.
notes: Case-linked coordination passage relevant; other generic crime reports on the page are excluded. Byline, opening headline and full context on 1A absent. Distinguish existing Precinct 1 from a proposed temporary/permanent north-end precinct; do not infer the proposed location was opened.

title: LEGACY — continuation from 1A (opening headline unavailable)
text:
[Continued from page 1A; first visible fragment: Investigation.]

Hamby and her family still believe the person responsible for Levi’s death can be found.

“This has got to be eating at somebody, so much so it affects your breathing with a heavy heart as it does ours,” she wrote. “God is the ultimate judge and God only knows.”

“We know Levi was calling for help and we can’t get the sound out of our ears.”

Hamby said Levi’s mother, Marilyn Hamby, and father, Milton Frady, still live in Forsyth County, though they are not together.

Levi’s twin sister Laci, now 21, lives with Janice Hamby.

Levi was last seen a decade ago on his bicycle leaving his friend’s house on Noah Road, not far away from his Burrus Mill Road home.

His bike and some shell casings were found in a ditch off Little Mill Road.

GBI agent John Cagle, who is handling the Frady case, declined last week to comment on whether any new evidence or methods had surfaced over the past decade.

“Anytime a case is that old, any case of this age has obstacles,” Cagle said. “We try to work through those and stay focused.”

Cagle said the GBI has remained in contact with Frady’s family, including his mother and sister.

Nearly five years after his death, Georgia established Levi’s Call in his memory.

The emergency alert system represents a partnership of state law enforcement, emergency management and news outlets.

Levi’s Call, the state’s version of the Amber Alert, notifies the public immediately after a confirmed child abduction.

“Whenever a Levi’s Call or an Amber Alert is issued, it kicks into play many different ways of getting out the message of the missing child,” Cagle said. “Prior to that, we didn’t have a method to do that.”

John Bankhead, spokesman for the Georgia Crime Information Center, said children have been found alive 66 of the 68 times Levi’s Call has been enacted.

The other two children, Bankhead said, had died prior to the alert.

Moss, who continues to work with the GBI on the matter, said Forsyth County has not had another case of an abducted child since Levi’s murder.

“It’s still an active investigation and there is information coming in regularly,” he said. “We refer that information to the GBI.

We take any missing kid case very seriously. We are reminded that anything can happen.”

title: Grandmother makes plea for reward fund donations in hopes of sparking more leads
author: Beth L. Chester
text:
Saying she fears the trail leading to her grandson’s assailant may be growing colder, Levi Frady’s grandmother Janice Hamby is asking for the community’s financial support to help catch the 11-year-old’s killer.

Levi was a sixth grader at North Forsyth Middle School when he was abducted while riding his bike Oct. 22, 1997. He was found shot to death the following day in the Dawson Forest wildlife management area of Dawson County.

Nine months later, Hamby is making a plea for businesses and individuals who have not already pledged contributions to the reward fund to do so. A higher reward might spur new leads in the case, she said.

The reward for information leading to an arrest and conviction in the case has remained at just more than $15,000 since the fund was established shortly after the murder.

Georgia Bureau of Investigation Special Agent-in-Charge Jim Hallman said this week that though he continues to have three agents assigned full-time to the case, the number of viable new leads coming in has greatly decreased.

At this time, Hallman said an arrest in the murder is not imminent.

The veteran agent said he continues to believe Levi’s killer will eventually be found. But before investigators can arrest the person or persons responsible, they need any individuals with the remaining pieces of information about the murder to come forward.

A larger reward, officials say, might help to bring those tips to the surface.

Already, more than three dozen Forsyth County businesses and several individuals have pledged $7,000 in contributions.

A $2,000 pledge from the Forsyth County Board of Commissioners and a $1,000 pledge from the Sheriff’s Office Crimestoppers unit brings the total from Forsyth County to $10,000.

In Dawson County, two businesses and several individuals pledged contributions to the reward. Four individuals pledged $500 each, with others making contributions between $20 and $250.

The $3,400 from Dawson residents is in addition to the $2,000 initial pledge from the Governor’s office.

Danny Hansard, part owner of Klub Kids, a Forsyth County child care center, said their organization made a $100 pledge to the fund last year because they believe it’s important for the community to do anything it can do to find justice for Levi.

“If it’s possible that something as simple as money would aid in the capture, I’m all for it,” Hansard said. “And any human being that has any compassion about this at all — I don’t see how they could feel any other way.”

Hansard said small businesses which can’t make large contributions should pledge as much as they can, realizing numerous $100 donations or less add up to thousands of dollars.

Dawson County business owner Paul Mincey pledged $300 on behalf of 400 Jewelry & Loan. Mincey said he knows first hand the devastation of murder.

Prior to the arrest and convictions of Stephen Mobley for the murder of a Domino’s Pizza worker in Oakwood several years ago, Mincey said he was a suspect in that murder. It was Mincey who returned from a pizza delivery to find his co-worker slain inside the restaurant.

Mincey said he pledged a contribution to help find Levi’s killer because “anyone who commits cold-blooded murder should be brought to justice.” He said he, too, believes somebody knows something about this murder.

As a business owner, Mincey said he donates to a variety of causes and “can’t think of anything more important than this.”

Levi’s grandmother said she and her husband will pledge money saying: “We can’t ask anyone else to give until we have given.”

Hamby said there is nothing else the family can do for Levi except try to find his killer. She said she also believes an increased reward may help other children as well by protecting them from her grandson’s assailant. In a letter about her request, Hamby wrote, “We can’t go on the assumption that it will not happen again. The price is too great.

“You can’t keep your children inside all summer, and you can’t be with them every minute, and it’s not fair that they have to be treated this way. We can’t stop all the dangers but we might can stop this one.”

She stressed the family’s appreciation for all the community has already done. “Levi can’t have died for nothing,” she said.

Pledges to the reward fund may be made by phone. Contributions may be collected when an arrest is made in the case. Those who want to pledge in Forsyth County may phone Sheriff’s Office spokesperson Karleen Chalker at (770) 781-3052. In Dawson County, phone (706) 265-2222.

Dawson County Sheriff Billy Carlisle said he continues to believe Levi’s murder was not the act of a random killer passing through the area. “I believe he was killed by someone who knew the Forsyth and Dawson county area very well,” he said. That belief is based in part on the fact that Levi was taken to a remote area of Dawson forest.

Others in law enforcement, as well as a spokesperson for the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, have said it is not common for child abduction murder victims to die as a result of gun shots wounds. Often, when a child is abducted and slain at random, molestation is involved, and victims die from strangulation or other close contact physical abuse.

Authorities still will not disclose whether Levi was molested, saying placing “guilty knowledge” information in the public domain would decrease the credibility of future leads and lessen the evidentiary value of potential statements in the case.

Though Dawson investigators are no longer assigned full time to the case, Carlisle said they continue to assist as needed. Agent Hallman with the GBI said the case will never be closed unless an arrest is made. He confirmed that shortly after the murder, agents ordered the Dawson Forest crime scene area to be clear cut and called in cadets from North Georgia College to assist in a thorough search for clues.

If you have information about Levi’s murder, call the Georgia Bureau of Investigation at (770) 535-5423 or the 24-hour hotline at (800) 432-9284. To remain anonymous, write: Levi Frady Case, P.O. Box 229, Dawsonville, Ga. 30534.
notes: Staff Writer. Photo/Tom Brooks caption: “Levi Frady’s grandmother would like to raise the reward amount in hopes of catching the killer.” Reward-sign photo displays $15,000.00; sign lettering is not substituted for article’s “just more than” amount. Generic child-homicide comments are not evidence about sexual assault in Levi’s case.

title: FAMILY — continuation from 1A (opening headline unavailable)
text:
Georgia Bureau of Investigation spokesman John Bankhead said Levi’s family had wanted to come forward for several weeks: “We had to persuade them not to do this for a while.”

More than anything else, Levi’s mother said she “just can’t understand why.”

Although Parkman said she is in disbelief that someone who knew Levi would have taken his life, that is exactly what she believes may have happened.

“I don’t believe he would have got in a car with a stranger,” she said, adding they had talked together about the importance of avoiding strangers “too many times.”

To the person responsible for the family’s tremendous loss, Hamby posed the question she hopes will someday be answered: “Why did you take him away from so many people who loved him? We need him so bad.”

The other grandchildren want to talk about Levi, she said, and can’t understand why he is gone: “We can’t explain it to them because we don’t know.

“If we could find out why,” Hamby said the family could help them understand.

Both Hamby and Parkman said they believe someone has information which can help them answer their questions and put the person responsible for Levi’s murder behind bars.

“Please just call and let somebody know.”
notes: Opening headline and byline absent. Photo/Tom Brooks caption: “At Friday’s family-called press conference, Janice Hamby, with her daughter, Marilyn Parkman, mother of Levi and Laci Frady.” Lower-left photo/Tom Brooks caption: “Portrait of the twins, at age 3, hangs as the room’s focal point.” These images are newspaper reproductions. Beliefs about familiarity with an offender are not eyewitness identifications.

title: He was only eleven, says poem penned by grandmother
text:
He was only eleven
So full of life and fun
Why do children have to pay
For things they’ve never done

He was only eleven
And had his whole future ahead
Birthday parties and school dances
But now he is dead

He was only eleven
He didn’t seem to have a care
But now when I go to get him
I realize he’s not there

He was only eleven
Are children easy prey?
They are so trusting
They believe what you say

He was only eleven
What did he have to give?
Not anything you wanted
Why didn’t you let him live?

He was only eleven
And everyone has to die
We’re happy he’s in Heaven
But missing him makes us cry
notes: Literary/family remembrance, not investigative evidence. Header attributes poem to grandmother but gives no separate byline; no authorship identity inferred beyond that. Stanzas read top-to-bottom in each printed column, then next column. No factual claims/events extracted from poetic statements.

title: Investigators hoping to ‘jog the memory’
author: Beth L. Chester
text:
During a Friday afternoon press conference, agents investigating the murder of young Levi Frady echoed the slain 11-year-old’s mother’s belief that “someone must have seen or heard something” the evening Levi disappeared.

Marilyn Parkman ended the family’s plea for help in bringing her son’s killer to justice with the words, “Please call.”

To help “jog the memory” of anyone who may have information in the case, Georgia Bureau of Investigation spokesperson John Bankhead wants to remind area residents of Oct. 22 — the day Levi went out for a ride on his bike.

“It was the night of the fifth game of the World Series,” he said, “and it was a Wednesday night, when people may have been going to prayer service.”

Perhaps most importantly, since Daylight Saving’s Time was still in effect, Bankhead pointed out that investigators believe Levi came into contact with his assailant(s) before the sun went down — sometime between 6 and 7 p.m.

That’s significant, he said, because it means someone “could have seen” the perpetrator on Little Mill Road before or after Levi was abducted. It’s also possible, he said, that someone noticed “a young boy in a car” elsewhere that evening.

He’s hoping the reminder will cause everyone to think back to that day, recall what he or she was doing and possibly remember even something seemingly insignificant which might help investigators solve the case.

Bankhead told reporters that Levi’s father, Milton Frady, who initially refused to come forward and answer questions about his son’s disappearance, had now “pretty much been ruled out” as a suspect.

When asked whether others in the family continue to be possible suspects, Bankhead replied, “I don’t feel that’s a significant aspect.”

As for the speculation that Levi was murdered as a means of retaliation against someone he was close to, the GBI spokesman would only say that agents “are not ruling out any possibility at this point.”

Bankhead said investigators from several regional GBI offices are working to solve the case and have thus far compiled 30 volumes of case files and pursued more than 500 leads.

Special Agent-in-Charge of the Gainesville GBI region, Jim Hallman, said agents have polygraphed at least 20 individuals in the case to date. He would not reveal the identity of those questioned or say whether anyone failed the exam.

Hallman and two other investigators returned last week from a lengthy consultation with behavioral scientists and other child abduction experts at the FBI training center in Virginia.

Anyone with any information is asked to call the Dawson County hotline at 800-432-9284, the GBI at 535-5423 or Forsyth County Crime Stoppers at 888-7308. For those who prefer not to speak directly to law enforcement, write to: Levi Frady Case, P.O. Box 229, Dawsonville, Ga. 30534.
notes: Staff Writer. Photo/Tom Brooks caption: “GBI spokesman John Bankhead offered points of reference.” A press conference on Friday is inferred as Dec. 19 from the Sunday Dec. 21 issue; inference recorded separately. The 6–7 p.m. window is investigative belief, not a precise abduction timestamp. Polygraph count does not establish reliability/results of any test. Historical investigative characterizations do not establish present status or guilt.

title: FRADY — continuation from 1A (opening headline unavailable)
text:
[Continued from page 1A; supplied text begins mid-sentence.]

then went home and fell asleep, assuming that he had spent the night at a friend’s house.

When Levi did not return home the next day, friends helped the family search. His twin sister found his bike in a ditch off Little Mill Road, a well-traveled two-lane road between Hwys. 306 and 369. The Forsyth County Sheriff’s Office was called, and personnel from several state and local agencies launched an urgent search.

However, it was hunters who, later that same Thursday, found Levi’s body some 15 miles away in the Dawson forest.

He had been shot to death.

The Georgia Bureau of Investigation and the sheriffs’ offices from both counties teamed up on the murder investigation, following tips and leads that led nowhere.

The physical evidence was “little to none,” Paxton said.

“There were a couple of shell casings,” he said.

Asked if any DNA evidence had been found on the boy’s body, the sheriff shook his head.

Investigators do not believe this was the act of a serial killer.

“A serial killer is a serial killer. You’ve got to have more than one,” Paxton said. “There is always going to be evidence to allow us to say this is the work of one person. The problem we had in the Levi Frady case is there had never been before or since another case like it.”

Based on the lack of other injuries to the body, there is no reason to believe that someone accidentally hit the child with a car as he was pedaling his bike and in an act of desperation tried to cover up the mishap by killing him, according to the sheriff.

And though the murder appears almost to have been execution-style, in the five years since the death, no motive for something like that has emerged.

Capt. Ron Freeman, commander of the sheriff’s office’s criminal investigations division, said Friday that new leads in the case continue to come in periodically.

“We were out doing interviews this week,” he said, adding that the interviews were for background information, not to interview any suspects.

“We’ve not targeted in on a specific suspect at this time,” Freeman said.

One of the new faces in the investigative team is that of John Cagle, the newly appointed special agent in charge of the Gainesville Regional Office of the GBI.

In an interview Friday afternoon, Cagle said the Frady case was the first one he picked up when he assumed his new position three weeks ago.

“I went to the crime scene yesterday, with our case agent,” Cagle said, adding that he also has read all 50 volumes of evidence in the case.

He reiterated that the killer is still being actively pursued.

“Although it’s an old case, and at least to this point unsolved and is discouraging certainly for family members and discouraging for the police officers who have — working on his case — believe me, they have really wrestled with it; a lot of the agents working on it have children of a similar age — I can assure the community over there, we’re still working this case as hard as we did when it first happened ... ”

“In fact, I had an agent today running down a lead on it,” Cagle said.

The one good thing that has come out of the tragedy is the creation of a statewide emergency alert system for abducted children that is called “Levi’s Call.”

According to Vicki Metz of the GBI Public Affairs Office, the program is a partnership of her agency, Georgia Emergency Management Agency and the Georgia Association of Broadcasters.

Recently, the Georgia Department of Transportation also has agreed to post alerts on its changeable message signs, Metz said.

“The name Levi’s Call came from us wanting to remember one of our own on behalf of all missing and murdered children in Georgia,” she added.

Only once has since its activation in January has the system been used. That was during a Florida child’s abduction in which the perpetrator brought the child to Georgia and, then, after Levi’s Call became activated, turned his car around and went back to Florida.

That child was returned unharmed.
notes: No byline/opening headline supplied. Pull quote duplicates Paxton passage: “The problem we had in the Levi Frady case is there had never been before or since another case like it.” Printed “Only once has since ...” retained. Paxton’s head-shake is the journalist’s observation, not a DNA lab report. Composite caption source credited “Georgia Bureau of Investigations” (as printed); it describes two possible witnesses, first seen Little Mill Road 6:30 p.m., late 50s, gray beard/blue cap/stooped; second white 45–55 clean-shaven slim 6 feet, white/gray hair, 1980–85 medium-blue Toyota pickup with white camper. Full caption retained separately below. No suspects identified.
caption: Investigators are seeking the public’s help in identifying two possible witnesses in the 1997 murder of Levi Frady. The first person was seen walking along Little Mill Road at 6:30 p.m. on the day the boy was first missed. The man is described as white in his late 50s, with a scruffy, gray beard. He was wearing a faded blue baseball cap. He walked in a stooped fashion. The second potential witness, right, was seen in the Dawson Forest Wildlife Management Area. He is described as white, 45-55, clean shaven, 6-feet tall, slim build with white or gray hair. He was driving a 1980 to 1985 medium blue Toyota, pick-up truck with a white camper shell over the bed of the vehicle. Anyone with information is asked to call (800) 432-9284 or by write: Levi Frady Case 189, Hwy.53 West, Suite 201, Dawsonville, GA 30534.

title: Frady reward offers glimmer of hope for new information
text:
The death of Levi Frady remains an injustice that haunts the Forsyth County community. Thanks to the generosity of two local businessmen, there is now a better chance of solving one of the county’s most horrific mysteries.

Last week, Tommy Bagwell, owner of American Proteins, and automobile dealer Bob Davis each agreed to add $50,000 to the reward being offered for information about the Levi Frady murder.

We can only hope that the addition of $100,000 to the existing reward fund, bringing the total to approximately $125,000, will provide the incentive necessary to unveil new clues in the murder.

A North Forsyth Middle School student, 11-year-old Levi disappeared while riding his bicycle Oct. 22, 1997. Deer hunters found his body the next day. The youngster had been shot to death.

Investigators from Dawson and Forsyth counties, as well as the GBI, have worked diligently to find the killer.

Forsyth County Sheriff Denny Hendrix recently formed a new task force to investigate Levi’s death, reviving interest in the case and resulting in the posting of the increased reward.

The newly promised reward money will be added to that already pledged by many others, including the governor’s office, Forsyth County Commission, Forsyth Sheriff’s Department, Dawson County officials and community leaders, and several private individuals.

The $100,000 added to the reward fund last week serves as a strong reminder that the case remains near to the hearts of many in Forsyth County and, at the same time, demonstrates the generosity and community spirit of the two individuals who have promised to make the funds available.

For that they are to be commended.

At the press conference announcing the new reward money, Bagwell noted that he has had a lengthy relationship with Frady family members.

“I have a long history with the family. I hope this helps,” Bagwell said.

Davis said he hoped his donation “helps bring justice to Levi Frady.”

So do we all.
notes: Unsigned editorial; class E rather than straight news C. Image captions: “Bob Davis”, “Tommy Bagwell”, portrait “Frady”. Approximate $125,000 is reported, not a ledger reconciliation. Pledges/agreements are not documented cash receipts. No guilt inferred from donor’s reported family association.
